01 · The challenge

Science is a hands-on subject. These students learn from home.

No lab bench

Students learn fully online, often with a parent or learning coach. Experiments, models and demonstrations had to work on a screen.

Reading is not learning

Existing lessons leaned on text and static images. Teachers saw students skim, click through and miss the core ideas.

Strict standards

Every lesson had to align to state science and health standards, meet accessibility rules, and fit the LMS's block-based authoring.

02 · My role

Lead learning designer, from standards to screens

I led lesson design for the science and health courses. I worked with US classroom teachers as subject experts and with our graphic designers to turn each standard into a lesson students do, not just read.

Standards mapping

Unpacked each standard with SMEs into objectives, misconceptions to target and evidence of learning.

Lesson blueprints

Planned each lesson's flow and chose the interaction that fit each objective best.

Storyboards

Wrote on-screen text, interaction logic, feedback and art briefs for the graphic designers.

Build and QA

Built lessons in the LMS and ran SME reviews, accessibility checks and functional QA.

04 · Design approach

Every lesson follows one arc: predict, explore, apply, check

The arc is inspired by the 5E model and fits the LMS's block structure. Students commit to an idea before they see the answer, which makes the explanation stick.

Predict

A real-world hook and a prediction the student commits to.

Explore

Simulations, hotspots and flip cards to discover the idea.

Apply

Sorting and scenarios set in students' everyday lives.

Check

Knowledge checks with feedback on every option.

05 · Interaction library

The right interaction for each objective

We built a shared library of patterns so designers, graphic artists and teachers spoke the same language. Each pattern had a template, art spec and accessibility notes.

Simulations

Change a variable and watch the result. Best for cause and effect.

Physics: force and acceleration lab

Labeled hotspots

Explore parts of a diagram one at a time, with a short explanation for each.

Biology: organelles of an animal cell

Flip cards

Recall first, then check. Good for laws, terms and definitions.

Physics: Newton's three laws

Sorting

Classify examples into groups, with tap-to-place for touch and keyboard users.

Biology: producers, consumers, decomposers

Process steps

Walk through a sequence stage by stage, with a visual for each step.

Biology: the stages of mitosis

Branching scenarios

Make a choice and see the consequence. Builds judgment, not just recall.

PE: planning a safe workout by heart-rate zone

Why it worked

Teachers in the room. Working with experienced US teachers kept lessons accurate and aimed at the misconceptions they saw every day.

Designers and artists together. Storyboards carried art briefs, so diagrams explained the idea instead of decorating the page.

A shared pattern library. Reusable interactions sped up builds and kept the experience consistent across three subjects.

08 · Reflection

What I learned

Interaction must earn its place

The best activities asked students to make a decision. Clicking to reveal text is not engagement. Predicting and then testing is.

Feedback is the teacher in the room

Online, the feedback message is the only teacher present at that moment. Writing feedback for each wrong answer was the highest-value time we spent.
